claim: Septins are a family of GTP-binding proteins that are highly conserved from yeast to mammalian cells.
source: Septins are a family of GTP-binding proteins that are highly conserved from yeast to mammalian cells (Longtine et al., 1996; Gladfelter et al., 2001; Cao et al., 2007; Nishihama et al., 2011; Onishi and Pringle, 2016; Marquardt et al., 2019; Woods and Gladfelter, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Septins form hetero-oligomeric complexes that can assemble into different higher-order structures such as rings, gauzes, hourglasses, bars.
source: They form hetero-oligomeric complexes that can assemble into different higher-order structures such as rings, gauzes, hourglasses, bars, and carry out various functions (Frazier et al., 1998; Hsu et al., 1998; Kinoshita, 2003; Sheffield et al., 2003; Bertin et al., 2008; Garcia et al., 2011; Bridges et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Septins can serve as scaffolds for protein recruitment at discrete cellular locations.
source: Septins can serve as scaffolds for protein recruitment at discrete cellular locations (Gladfelter et al., 2001; Versele and Thorner, 2005; Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Finnigan et al., 2015; Meitinger and Palani, 2016; Perez et al., 2016; Marquardt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Septins are proposed to act as a diffusion barrier to ensure that cellular components are spatially segregated or compartmentalized.
source: Septins are proposed to act as a diffusion barrier to ensure that cellular components are spatially segregated or compartmentalized (Dobbelaere and Barral, 2004; Caudron and Barral, 2009; Hu and Nelson, 2011; McMurray et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature and uses the term 'proposed', indicating it is a hypothesis supported by prior work.

claim: Septins can sense membrane curvatures and/or deform the plasma membrane due to their lipid-binding properties.
source: They can also sense the membrane curvatures and/or deform the plasma membrane due to their lipid-binding properties (Bridges and Gladfelter, 2016; Cannon et al., 2017; Cannon et al., 2019; McMurray, 2019; Shi et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Septins are involved in multiple processes including cytokinesis, mitosis, exocytosis, apoptosis, fungal or viral infections, neuronal spine morphogenesis, ciliogenesis, and spermiogenesis.
source: The diverse roles of septins lead to their involvement in multiple processes including cytokinesis, mitosis, exocytosis, apoptosis, fungal or viral infections, neuronal spine morphogenesis, ciliogenesis, and spermiogenesis (Longtine et al., 1996; Kartmann and Roth, 2001; Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Dolat et al., 2014; Momany and Talbot, 2017; Ageta-Ishihara and Kinoshita, 2021; Neubauer and Zieger, 2021; Woods and Gladfelter, 2021; Safavian et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The septin ring or hourglass structures at the presumptive bud site and bud neck are required for the recruitment and maintenance of various cytokinesis proteins in budding yeast.
source: The septin ring or hourglass structures at the presumptive bud site and bud neck are required for the recruitment and maintenance of various cytokinesis proteins (Bi et al., 1998; Lippincott and Li, 1998; Gladfelter et al., 2001; Longtine and Bi, 2003; Marquardt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Budding yeast septins recruit proteins through direct interactions with proteins such as the F-BAR protein Hof1.
source: These roles occur through either direct interactions with proteins such as the F-BAR protein Hof1 (Vallen et al., 2000; Meitinger et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2013), or through septin-binding proteins such as Bni5, which links septins to the myosin-II heavy chain Myo1 (Lee et al., 2002; Fang et al., 2010; Finnigan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Budding yeast septins recruit proteins through septin-binding proteins such as Bni5, which links septins to the myosin-II heavy chain Myo1.
source: These roles occur through either direct interactions with proteins such as the F-BAR protein Hof1 (Vallen et al., 2000; Meitinger et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2013), or through septin-binding proteins such as Bni5, which links septins to the myosin-II heavy chain Myo1 (Lee et al., 2002; Fang et al., 2010; Finnigan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The septin double rings were proposed to function as a diffusion barrier for proteins such as the exocyst component Sec3 and chitin synthase II (Chs2) at the division site in budding yeast.
source: During cytokinesis, the septin double rings were proposed to function as a diffusion barrier for proteins such as the exocyst component Sec3 and chitin synthase II (Chs2) at the division site (Dobbelaere and Barral, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and uses the term 'proposed', indicating it is a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: Other studies have challenged the view that septins function as a diffusion barrier by showing that Chs2 localizes efficiently to the division site in the absence of septin rings.
source: But other studies have challenged this view by showing that Chs2 localizes efficiently to the division site in the absence of septin rings (Wloka et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: No physical interactions between septins and the exocyst have been reported in budding yeast, even in genome-wide interactome studies.
source: However, no physical interactions between septins and the exocyst have been reported, even in the genome-wide interactome studies (Michaelis et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Septins are not essential in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: Unlike in budding yeast, septins are not essential in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, and their roles in cytokinesis remain obscure (Longtine et al., 1996; Berlin et al., 2003; Tasto et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast has seven septins, Spn1–Spn7, with Spn1–Spn4 expressing in vegetative cells and functioning at the division site.
source: Fission yeast has seven septins, Spn1–Spn7, with Spn1–Spn4 expressing in vegetative cells and functioning at the division site (Longtine et al., 1996; Berlin et al., 2003; Tasto et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2003; An et al., 2004; Petit et al., 2005; Onishi et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: None of the septins Spn1–Spn4 is essential in fission yeast, but loss of some or all of them causes a delay in cell separation, resulting in a multiseptated phenotype.
source: None of the septins Spn1–Spn4 is essential, but loss of some or all of them causes a delay in cell separation, resulting in a multiseptated phenotype (An et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Spn1 and Spn4 are the more important components of the septin ring structure during cytokinesis in fission yeast.
source: Spn1 and Spn4 are the more important components of the septin ring structure during cytokinesis (An et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast septins accumulate to the division site shortly before the contractile ring constriction and form a single ring which quickly transitions into unconstricting double rings.
source: Septins accumulate to the division site shortly before the contractile ring constriction and form a single ring which quickly transitions into unconstricting double rings (Berlin et al., 2003; Tasto et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast septins recruit the anillin Mid2 to the division site.
source: It is only known that septins recruit the anillin Mid2 (Berlin et al., 2003; Tasto et al., 2003), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Gef3 (Muñoz et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015), the small GTPase Rho4 (Wang et al., 2015), and the glucanases Eng1 and Agn1 to the division site (Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast septins recruit the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Gef3 to the division site.
source: It is only known that septins recruit the anillin Mid2 (Berlin et al., 2003; Tasto et al., 2003), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Gef3 (Muñoz et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015), the small GTPase Rho4 (Wang et al., 2015), and the glucanases Eng1 and Agn1 to the division site (Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast septins recruit the small GTPase Rho4 to the division site.
source: It is only known that septins recruit the anillin Mid2 (Berlin et al., 2003; Tasto et al., 2003), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Gef3 (Muñoz et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015), the small GTPase Rho4 (Wang et al., 2015), and the glucanases Eng1 and Agn1 to the division site (Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast septins recruit the glucanases Eng1 and Agn1 to the division site.
source: It is only known that septins recruit the anillin Mid2 (Berlin et al., 2003; Tasto et al., 2003), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Gef3 (Muñoz et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015), the small GTPase Rho4 (Wang et al., 2015), and the glucanases Eng1 and Agn1 to the division site (Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that septins function in exocytosis.
source: Previous studies have suggested that septins function in exocytosis (Hsu et al., 1998; Vega and Hsu, 2003; Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2005; Pérez et al., 2015; Tokhtaeva et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast septins are proposed to work with the exocyst complex to regulate the secretion of glucanases at the appropriate location.
source: Fission yeast septins are proposed to work with the exocyst complex to regulate the secretion of glucanases at the appropriate location, but it was reported that septins and the exocyst are independent for localization (Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2005; Pérez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and uses the term 'proposed', indicating it is a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: It was reported that septins and the exocyst are independent for localization in fission yeast.
source: Fission yeast septins are proposed to work with the exocyst complex to regulate the secretion of glucanases at the appropriate location, but it was reported that septins and the exocyst are independent for localization (Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2005; Pérez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The exocyst is a highly conserved, octameric complex (Sec3, Sec5, Sec6, Sec8, Sec10, Sec15, Exo70, and Exo84) in exocytosis.
source: The exocyst is a highly conserved, octameric complex (Sec3, Sec5, Sec6, Sec8, Sec10, Sec15, Exo70, and Exo84) in exocytosis (TerBush et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2002; Hsu et al., 2004; Heider and Munson, 2012; Liu and Guo, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The exocyst functions in late stages of exocytosis by promoting the tethering and fusion of post-Golgi secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane.
source: It functions in late stages of exocytosis by promoting the tethering and fusion of post-Golgi secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane (TerBush et al., 1996; Hsu et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Studies suggest that septins regulate the exocyst complex and a possible involvement of septins in targeting secretory vesicles to the exocytic sites.
source: Although studies suggest that septins regulate the exocyst complex and a possible involvement of septins in targeting secretory vesicles to the exocytic sites (Hsu et al., 1998; Vega and Hsu, 2003; Li et al., 2007; Gupta et al., 2015), no direct physical interactions between septins and the exocyst subunits have been reported in budding yeast or other organisms except rat brain (Hsu et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: No direct physical interactions between septins and the exocyst subunits have been reported in budding yeast or other organisms except rat brain.
source: Although studies suggest that septins regulate the exocyst complex and a possible involvement of septins in targeting secretory vesicles to the exocytic sites (Hsu et al., 1998; Vega and Hsu, 2003; Li et al., 2007; Gupta et al., 2015), no direct physical interactions between septins and the exocyst subunits have been reported in budding yeast or other organisms except rat brain (Hsu et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Spn1 and Sec3 colocalized at the division site as a single ring first, and later as double rings during septum formation.
source: Spn1 and Sec3 colocalized at the division site as a single ring first, and later as double rings during septum formation (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The colocalization of Spn1 with another exocyst subunit Exo70 was confirmed using SoRa spinning disk confocal microscopy.
source: The colocalization of Spn1 with another exocyst subunit Exo70 was confirmed using SoRa (Super resolution by Optical Re-Assignment) spinning disk confocal microscopy (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C using SoRa microscopy.

claim: Sec3 and Exo70, but not Spn1, also concentrated at cell tips.
source: Sec3 and Exo70, but not Spn1, also concentrated at cell tips (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Sec3 arrived at the division site 13.4 ± 2.2 min after spindle pole body separation.
source: However, Sec3 arrived at the division site 13.4 ± 2.2 min after spindle pole body separation, about 10 min earlier than Spn1, which arrived at 23.6 ± 1.8 min (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Spn1 arrived at the division site at 23.6 ± 1.8 min after spindle pole body separation.
source: However, Sec3 arrived at the division site 13.4 ± 2.2 min after spindle pole body separation, about 10 min earlier than Spn1, which arrived at 23.6 ± 1.8 min (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Sec3 appeared at the division site about 10 min earlier than Spn1.
source: However, Sec3 arrived at the division site 13.4 ± 2.2 min after spindle pole body separation, about 10 min earlier than Spn1, which arrived at 23.6 ± 1.8 min (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Time-lapse movies of Exo70-tdTomato and Spn1-mEGFP confirmed that the exocyst appeared at the division site earlier than septins.
source: Time-lapse movies of Exo70-tdTomato and Spn1-mEGFP confirmed that the exocyst appeared at the division site earlier than septins (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1—video 1.

claim: In WT cells, Spn1 always formed ring structures at the rim of division plane during septation.
source: In WT cells, Spn1 always formed ring structures at the rim of division plane during septation (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In exocyst mutants exo70Δ and the temperature-sensitive sec3-913 and sec8-1, Spn1 localization was comparable to WT at permissive temperature.
source: In exocyst mutants exo70Δ and the temperature-sensitive sec3-913 and sec8-1, Spn1 localization was comparable to WT at permissive temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At the restrictive temperature, a fraction of Spn1 abnormally spread onto the division plane following furrow ingression in sec3-913 and sec8-1 mutants.
source: At the restrictive temperature, although Spn1 localized as a ring at the division site before septation, a fraction of Spn1 abnormally spread onto the division plane following furrow ingression in sec3-913 and sec8-1 mutants (Figure 1F, red boxes; and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, middle focal plane).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only minor mislocalization of Spn1 was observed in exo70Δ cells even at 36°C.
source: Only minor mislocalization of Spn1 was observed in exo70Δ cells even at 36°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Some Spn1 followed the contractile ring marked with Rng8 as it constricted, spread onto the new plasma membrane, and concentrated at the center of the division plane while maintaining its localization at the rim.
source: Indeed, some Spn1 followed the contractile ring marked with Rng8 (Wang et al., 2014) as it constricted, spread onto the new plasma membrane, and concentrated at the center of the division plane while maintaining its localization at the rim (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G and a citation.

claim: Spn1 levels were comparable or higher in exocyst mutants compared to WT at both 25 and 36°C.
source: Spn1 levels were comparable or higher in exocyst mutants compared to WT at both 25 and 36°C (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: FRAP analyses of Spn1 showed no difference in its dynamics in WT and sec3-913 cells at 36°C.
source: FRAP analyses of Spn1 showed no difference in its dynamics in WT and sec3-913 cells at 36°C (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Septins only partially depend on the exocyst for their localization.
source: Collectively, despite some Spn1 mislocalizing to the center of the division plane in exocyst mutants, the majority of Spn1 still localizes to the rim. Thus, septins only partially depend on the exocyst for their localization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localization data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: In mitotic cells without a septum, the exocyst localized to the rim of the division plane in both WT and spn1Δ cells.
source: In mitotic cells without a septum, the exocyst localized to the rim of the division plane in both WT and spn1Δ cells (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, yellow boxes).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: During septation, the exocyst spread across the division plane as a disk in spn1Δ cells while it remained at the rim in WT cells.
source: During septation, however, the exocyst spread across the division plane as a disk in spn1Δ cells while it remained at the rim in WT cells (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, red boxes).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The levels of Sec3, Exo70, and Sec8 at the division site in spn1Δ cells were not significantly different from WT before septation.
source: The levels of Sec3, Exo70, and Sec8 at the division site in spn1Δ cells were not significantly different from WT before septation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: During and after septum formation, the levels of all three exocyst components were significantly reduced at the division site (except Exo70 in cells with forming septum) and almost absent at the rim in spn1Δ cells.
source: During and after septum formation, the levels of all three exocyst components were significantly reduced at the division site (except Exo70 in cells with forming septum) and almost absent at the rim in spn1Δ cells (Figure 2A, B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The dynamics of Sec3 at the division site was not affected in spn1Δ cells.
source: However, the dynamics of Sec3 at the division site was not affected in spn1Δ cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The exocyst was much more dynamic than septins at the division site.
source: The exocyst was much more dynamic than septins at the division site (Figures 1H and 2C), which was confirmed by high temporal resolution imaging of Exo70 (Figure 1—videos 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1H, 2C and Figure 1—videos 2 and 3.

claim: Loss of septins results in exocyst mislocalization and its decreased levels, especially at the rim of the division plane during septum formation.
source: Together, loss of septins results in exocyst mislocalization and its decreased levels, especially at the rim of the division plane during septum formation, suggesting that septins play an important role in regulating the exocyst localization at the division site.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localization and quantification data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Septins play an important role in regulating the exocyst localization at the division site.
source: Together, loss of septins results in exocyst mislocalization and its decreased levels, especially at the rim of the division plane during septum formation, suggesting that septins play an important role in regulating the exocyst localization at the division site.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localization and quantification data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Spn1 ring localization was not affected in rho4Δ gef3Δ cells.
source: We found that Spn1 ring localization was not affected in rho4Δ gef3Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Although partially mislocalized to the center of the division plane, the majority of Sec3 still localized as a ring at the rim of the division plane in rho4Δ, gef3Δ, and rho4Δ gef3Δ cells.
source: Although partially mislocalized to the center of the division plane, the majority of Sec3 still localized as a ring at the rim of the division plane in rho4Δ, gef3Δ, and rho4Δ gef3Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The different localization patterns of the exocyst in spn1Δ and rho4Δ gef3Δ cells suggest that septins can regulate exocyst localization independent of Gef3 and Rho4.
source: Thus, the different localization patterns of the exocyst in spn1Δ and rho4Δ gef3Δ cells suggest that septins can regulate exocyst localization independent of Gef3 and Rho4.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localization data comparing spn1Δ and rho4Δ gef3Δ cells.

claim: No physical interactions were detected among Spn1–Sec3, Spn1–Exo70, Spn4–Sec3, and Spn4–Exo70 using co-immunoprecipitation of cell extracts from fission yeast.
source: Therefore, we first tested the interactions between Spn1–Sec3, Spn1–Exo70, Spn4–Sec3, and Spn4–Exo70 using co-immunoprecipitation of cell extracts from fission yeast. Surprisingly, no physical interactions were detected among the four proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: AlphaFold2_advanced ColabFold algorithm was used to predict the physical interactions between all 32 combinations of the four septins and eight exocyst subunits.
source: Then we utilized AlphaFold2_advanced ColabFold algorithm (Jumper et al., 2021; Mirdita et al., 2022), whose highly accurate predictions of protein structures have revolutionized structural biology, to predict the physical interactions between all 32 combinations of the four septins and eight exocyst subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by the use of AlphaFold2 for computational predictions, with citations to the algorithm.

claim: The top six predicted interactions between the septin and exocyst subunits are: Spn2 and Sec15, Sec15 and Spn1, Sec6 and Spn1, Spn2 and Sec5, Spn4 and Sec15, and Spn4 and Sec3.
source: Based on the above analyses, we predicted the following top six interactions between the septin and exocyst subunits: Spn2 and Sec15 (Figure 3), Sec15 and Spn1, Sec6 and Spn1, Spn2 and Sec5, Spn4 and Sec15, and Spn4 and Sec3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AlphaFold2 predictions shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 84% of exocyst and 96% of septin predicted interacting residues were sterically feasible without disrupting the architecture of exocyst or septin complex.
source: Our analyses revealed that 84% of exocyst and 96% of septin predicted interacting residues were sterically feasible without disrupting the architecture of exocyst or septin complex (the residues highlighted in yellow in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Figure 3—video 1; Figure 3—video 2), while others would likely require partial disassembly or flexible conformations.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and videos.

claim: Spn2 physically interacted with Sec15 and Sec5.
source: We found that Spn2 physically interacted with Sec15 and Sec5, Spn1 with Sec15 and Sec6, and Spn4 with Sec15 (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spn1 physically interacted with Sec15 and Sec6.
source: We found that Spn2 physically interacted with Sec15 and Sec5, Spn1 with Sec15 and Sec6, and Spn4 with Sec15 (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spn4 physically interacted with Sec15.
source: We found that Spn2 physically interacted with Sec15 and Sec5, Spn1 with Sec15 and Sec6, and Spn4 with Sec15 (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sec15 interacted with three septins Spn1, Spn2, and Spn4, which were stronger than other combinations.
source: Sec15 interacted with three septins Spn1, Spn2, and Spn4, which were stronger than other combinations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the Co-IP data presented.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid assays confirmed five pairs of interactions between septins and the exocyst.
source: We also utilized yeast two-hybrid assays to confirm these five pairs of interactions (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: X-gal overlay assay and quantification of β-galactosidase using o-nitrophenyl-β-D-galactopyranoside (ONPG) suggested that Sec15 may directly interact with Spn1, Spn2, and Spn4.
source: X-gal overlay assay (insets) and quantification of β-galactosidase using o-nitrophenyl-β-D-galactopyranoside (ONPG) suggested that Sec15 may directly interact with Spn1, Spn2, and Spn4 (Figure 4E); and Sec6 interacted with Spn1 through its C-terminal fragment (Spn1[300–469]) that contains the coiled-coil motif (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Sec6 interacted with Spn1 through its C-terminal fragment (Spn1[300–469]) that contains the coiled-coil motif.
source: X-gal overlay assay (insets) and quantification of β-galactosidase using o-nitrophenyl-β-D-galactopyranoside (ONPG) suggested that Sec15 may directly interact with Spn1, Spn2, and Spn4 (Figure 4E); and Sec6 interacted with Spn1 through its C-terminal fragment (Spn1[300–469]) that contains the coiled-coil motif (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Septins physically and likely directly interact with the exocyst in fission yeast via multivalent interactions.
source: Thus, we conclude that septins physically and likely directly interact with the exocyst in fission yeast via multivalent interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the Co-IP and yeast two-hybrid data presented.

claim: The deletion of spn1 or spn4 led to mislocalization of Sec15 on the division plane in ~75% of cells with a septum.
source: Indeed, similar to the results presented in Figures 1 and 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with other exocyst subunits, the deletion of spn1 or spn4 led to mislocalization of Sec15 on the division plane in ~75% of cells with a septum while Sec15 in ~90% of WT cells localized as rings at the rim of the division plane in septating cells (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Sec15 in ~90% of WT cells localized as rings at the rim of the division plane in septating cells.
source: Indeed, similar to the results presented in Figures 1 and 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with other exocyst subunits, the deletion of spn1 or spn4 led to mislocalization of Sec15 on the division plane in ~75% of cells with a septum while Sec15 in ~90% of WT cells localized as rings at the rim of the division plane in septating cells (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: In spn2Δ cells, Sec15 and Sec5 localized normally at the division site before septation.
source: Consistently, in spn2Δ cells, Sec15 and Sec5 localized normally at the division site before septation (Figure 5A, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: Both Sec15 and Sec5 spread more or less to the whole division plane in ~50% of spn2Δ cells with obvious septa.
source: Both Sec15 and Sec5 spread more or less to the whole division plane in ~50% of spn2Δ cells with obvious septa (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: Unlike in spn1Δ or spn4Δ cells, a fraction of Sec15 and Sec5 still localized to the rim in spn2Δ cells with a septum.
source: Unlike in spn1Δ or spn4Δ cells, a fraction of Sec15 and Sec5 still localized to the rim in spn2Δ cells with a septum (Figure 5A, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: Spn1, Spn2, and Spn4 are important for targeting the exocyst to the rim of division plane during cytokinesis through physical interactions.
